title: AcornSys heartbeat kernel profiling: TensorRT vs vLLM
topics: KV cache eviction and heartbeat traffic
summary: Deep dive with AcornSys on GPU runtime profiling. Primary asks: unpredictable p99 spikes under sustained traffic, occasional CUDA graph replay failures, and unexpected KV cache eviction during their heartbeat/keepalive traffic. Redwood SE explained kernel routing heuristics, multi-path execution, and tradeoffs between TensorRT-LLM and vLLM under mixed short/long prompt workloads. Agreed next steps: run customer-provided microbench on a Redwood probe cluster, share kernel-level NVTX traces and a perf spreadsheet, and propose pilot config for VPC deployment with conservative CUDA-graph fallback settings.
transcript:
[00:00] Alex Morgan: Okay everyone, thanks for joining. We're gonna do a focused profiling session — we saw the traces you sent and some spikes around p99 so want to walk through kernel handoff and cuda-graph replay behavior.

[00:18] Maya Chen: Yeah thanks, um, appreciate you doing this. The spikes happen during our heartbeat traffic — basically a 256-token prompt followed by a bunch of 8-token quick checks, and then the cache seems to... evict? then throughput drops.

[00:34] Samir Patel: Right, Two things to call out up front: one is the kernel-path tiebreaker in our runtime — when we see mixed sequence-lengths the runtime may pick a fast kernel optimized for long context and then switch back, and second is cudaGraph replay instability when the launch sequence changes mid-flight. Both can create latency jitter.

[00:58] Jon Rivera: Is that more TensorRT-LLM behavior or vLLM? We are running both in experiments.

[01:07] Priya Nair: Good question. TensorRT-LLM has more aggressive fused kernels and often uses static cudaGraph replay to accelerate steady-state long sequences — which is great for long chats but brittle when sequence shapes change. vLLM is more dynamic, it favors smaller kernels and more memcopies but is more tolerant to shape variability.

[01:36] Ethan Lowe: We saw some cudaGraph replay errors in our logs — the replay would abort then fallback to a slower path which caused a 200–400ms p99 blip. Is that what you're describing?

[01:51] Samir Patel: Exactly. When graph capture assumptions are invalidated (different batch or KV cache stride) the driver can return an error and the runtime falls back to multi-kernel execution. That fallback is correct but expensive.

[02:08] Ritika Shah: Our heartbeat traffic is somewhat rhythmic, like 1 request per second per client, but a small percent are longer. Could batching windows be adjusted or the heartbeat isolated?

[02:20] Alex Morgan: Yes — two approaches: isolate heartbeats onto a separate routing lane (so they don't break steady-state graph captures) or use conservative graph capture windows with deterministic fallback thresholds. Both have cost tradeoffs.

[02:40] [03:00] -- brief screen-share start (Samir)
notes: Screen-share included NVTX traces + sample CUDA graph error log. Customer uploaded: perf.zip (nvprof-like traces), heartbeat-sample.json, and a kube manifest. References: doc: /redwood/internal/traces/ff-acorn-2028-02 and shared sheet: https://go.redwood/perf-acorn-2028
